name: The Foot household — a documented grocer in a reconstructed household (south division)
head: inf_grocer_south_01

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_south_c2_007 is an anonymous reconstructed roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: THE SAME BUILDING. recon_1835_south_c2_007 is a shop or house that this layer reads as both workplace and dwelling - the schedule's store-residence and boarding-house families are exactly that, and a frontier tradesman living over his own premises is the type rather than the exception.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: S. Foot

occupation.note: THE PAPERS NAME HIM A GROCER. 1833-11-26 c016 (p. 3, col. 4): “GROCERIES. W[ines,] BRANDY, GIN, RUM, &c. &c. 20 Barrels Ohio Whiskey. 4[0] do. Ohio Sup[e]rfine Flour. 4 do. B[uc]k Wheat Flour. 3 do. Crackers. [1]8 do. Mackinac White Fish. 40 Bushels Dried Apples. Table Salt, Tin Ware, &c. for [s]ale by S. FOOT. Chicago, No[v]. [2]6, 1833.”. The corpus names him 1 time(s), 1833-11-26 to 1833-11-26. THE HOUSEHOLD'S OWN ARGUMENT IS UNCHANGED and is why this roof is in the dataset at all: One grocer is documented against fifty-two store and mixed-use roofs in the building schedule. Groceries - flour, salt, whisky, tea, candles - are the commonest small trade in a supply town. Four grocer households are inferred, placed toward the river and the built streets where the schedule puts its C-family store roofs, and three of them live over the shop, which is what the schedule's C2 'store-residence' family means.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON IN A RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD, AND THE TWO HALVES OF THAT ARE GRADED SEPARATELY. The person is real and the papers name him: 1833-11-26 c016 (p. 3, col. 4), and 1 mention(s) between 1833-11-26 and 1833-11-26. WHERE HE LIVED AND WORKED IS STILL RECONSTRUCTED — the dwelling, the workplace and the division on this record are the ones the inferred-household programme dealt to the invented resident this replaces, and NOTHING HERE CLAIMS THEY ARE HIS. No source this project holds gives him an address; if one did, the register would have placed him and tools/retire_invented_residents.py would have refused him for that reason (refusal 5). This is what T-0264 retires: the town raised this household because it demonstrably needed the trade and had nobody documented to put in it, and it now has somebody. The invented name and its `name_basis` are gone with the invention. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the liberty taken is the housing, not the man.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - first of 4 grocer households in this layer, in the south division. One grocer is documented against fifty-two store and mixed-use roofs in the building schedule. Groceries - flour, salt, whisky, tea, candles - are the commonest small trade in a supply town. Four grocer households are inferred, placed toward the river and the built streets where the schedule puts its C-family store roofs, and three of them live over the shop, which is what the schedule's C2 'store-residence' family means. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one.
